title: Oscillations, Waves and Sound
lines: USAT asks about simple harmonic motion (periods of a spring and a pendulum, speed and energy at a point), wave equations, the speed of sound, stationary waves in strings and pipes, beats, intensity level in decibels and the Doppler effect. Most questions turn on a proportion: what happens to the period, frequency or energy when one quantity is doubled or quadrupled.
## Simple harmonic motion
A body moves in SHM when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement and always directed towards the mean position: a = −ω²x.
- Displacement x = x₀ sin ωt, where x₀ is the amplitude and ω = 2πf = 2π/T.
- Speed v = ω√(x₀² − x²): greatest (ωx₀) at the mean position, zero at the extremes.
- Acceleration is greatest (ω²x₀) at the extremes and zero at the mean position.
- Energy: total E = ½kx₀², shared between kinetic and potential energy. Doubling the amplitude makes the energy four times as large.
| System | Period | Does not depend on
| Mass on a spring | T = 2π√(m/k) | g, amplitude
| Simple pendulum | T = 2π√(l/g) | mass, amplitude (small swings)
- A seconds pendulum (T = 2 s) is about 1 m long.
- On the Moon g is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so a pendulum's period grows by √6; a spring's period does not change.
> Example 1. A 0.5 kg mass hangs on a spring of constant 200 N/m. Find its period.
## Damping and resonance
- Free oscillations happen at the natural frequency. Damping (friction, air drag) makes the amplitude die away.
- Forced oscillations follow the driving frequency. Resonance: when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, the amplitude is greatest.
- Examples: tuning a radio circuit, a microwave oven heating water, a bridge set swinging by marching soldiers.
## Waves
- Wave equation: v = fλ. The frequency is set by the source and does not change when the wave enters a new medium; the speed and wavelength change.
- Transverse waves (light, waves on a string) vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel and can be polarised. Longitudinal waves (sound) vibrate along it and cannot be polarised.
- Speed of a wave on a string: v = √(T/μ), where T is the tension and μ is the mass per unit length.
- Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.
## Sound
- Sound needs a medium; it is fastest in solids and slowest in gases.
- Newton assumed isothermal changes and found about 280 m/s in air, which is too low. Laplace's correction (adiabatic changes) gives v = √(γP/ρ) ≈ 332 m/s at 0 °C.
- v is proportional to √T (T in kelvin). Changing the pressure at constant temperature does not change the speed. Sound travels faster in moist air than in dry air.
- Near room temperature, v rises by about 0.61 m/s for each 1 °C.
- Intensity level L = 10 log(I/I₀) decibels, with I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m². Every tenfold increase in intensity adds 10 dB.
- Loudness depends on intensity, pitch on frequency and quality (timbre) on the overtones present.
## Stationary waves
Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions form a stationary wave. Nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and the next antinode are λ/4 apart.
| System | Fundamental | Harmonics present
| String fixed at both ends | v/2L | all: f, 2f, 3f …
| Pipe open at both ends | v/2L | all: f, 2f, 3f …
| Pipe closed at one end | v/4L | odd only: f, 3f, 5f …
> Example 2. A pipe closed at one end is 0.25 m long. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, find its fundamental frequency and the next frequency it can produce.
> f₁ = v/4L = 340 ÷ 1.0 = 340 Hz. A closed pipe gives only odd harmonics, so the next is 3 × 340 = 1,020 Hz.
## Beats
Two notes of slightly different frequency produce beats at a rate equal to the difference: f(beats) = |f₁ − f₂|. Loading a tuning fork with wax lowers its frequency; filing it raises it.
> Example 3. A fork of 256 Hz gives 4 beats per second with an unknown fork. When the unknown fork is loaded with wax, the beat rate falls to 2 per second. Find the unknown frequency.
> It is 256 + 4 = 260 Hz or 256 − 4 = 252 Hz. Wax lowers its frequency; the beats fall only if it moves closer to 256 Hz, so it was 260 Hz.
## Doppler effect
The observed frequency changes when the source or the observer moves along the line joining them (v = speed of sound).
- Source approaching at u: f′ = fv/(v − u). Receding: f′ = fv/(v + u).
- Observer approaching at u: f′ = f(v + u)/v. Receding: f′ = f(v − u)/v.
- Uses: radar speed guns, sonar, blood-flow measurement, the red shift of receding galaxies.
> Example 4. An ambulance siren of 680 Hz approaches a standing listener at 20 m/s. Speed of sound 340 m/s. What frequency is heard?
! Pendulum period goes as √l: four times the length doubles the period, it does not quadruple it.
! A closed pipe's first overtone is the third harmonic (3f), not 2f.
! A source moving and an observer moving at the same speed do not give the same shift; use the right formula.
## Quick check
- Where is speed greatest in SHM? (at the mean position)
- Amplitude tripled: energy of oscillation? (nine times)
- Intensity multiplied by 100: change in intensity level? (+20 dB)
- Can sound waves be polarised? (no, they are longitudinal)
- Pendulum taken to the Moon: period? (longer, by √6)
